meta.subject: MICROECONOMICS
meta.author: bank-team-microeconomics
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify when marginal utility begins to fall
questions.stem: In a software team's ticket, a developer snacks on cookies while coding and rates each cookie's added satisfaction; which statement captures diminishing marginal utility?

options.text: The first cookie gives 10 utils and the second gives 8 utils, so extra satisfaction falls.
The first cookie gives 10 utils and the second gives 12 utils, so satisfaction always rises.
options.misconception: assumes utility always increases with quantity

options.text: Total utility stays flat at 10 utils no matter how many cookies are eaten.
Marginal utility equals price for every cookie, so no change occurs.
options.misconception: misapplies the equals-price rule to every unit

questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the previous one. The tempting claim that utility always rises ignores satiation; total utility need not stay flat.
questions.hint: Compare the extra satisfaction of successive units.

questions.stem: A tester logs total utility of 40 utils after four coffees and marginal utility of 6 for the fourth; what is total utility after three coffees?

options.text: 40 utils, because total utility never changes between cups.
options.misconception: treats total utility as constant across units

options.text: 46 utils, found by adding the fourth coffee's marginal utility instead.
options.misconception: adds instead of subtracts the marginal unit

options.text: 34 utils, found by subtracting the fourth coffee's marginal utility.
6 utils, confusing the marginal figure with the total level.
options.misconception: equates marginal utility with total utility

questions.explanation: Total utility after three cups equals total after four minus the fourth cup's marginal utility, giving 34 utils. Adding or freezing the total would misread the relationship.
questions.hint: Subtract the last unit's marginal contribution.

questions.stem: A programmer spends 4 dollars on a snack with marginal utility 20 utils; what is the marginal utility per dollar?
questions.explanation: Divide marginal utility by price: 20 utils divided by 4 dollars equals 5 utils per dollar. The result measures satisfaction per dollar spent.
questions.hint: Divide utils by dollars.

questions.stem: In a ticket about a designer buying pens, the rule that maximizes utility subject to budget is which of the following?

options.text: Spend all income on the cheapest good available in the store.
Equalize marginal utility per dollar across all goods purchased.
options.misconception: states a partial version of the rule

options.text: Maximize total utility without regard to prices paid.
Buy until marginal utility equals price for every good bought.

questions.explanation: The consumer maximizes utility by buying units until marginal utility equals price for each good purchased. Equalizing per dollar alone is incomplete, and ignoring prices or budgets is wrong.
questions.hint: The stopping condition involves price.

questions.learningObjective: Compute total utility from marginal values
questions.stem: A QA engineer records marginal utilities of 12, 9, 7 and 4 utils for four test runs; what is total utility?
questions.explanation: Total utility is the sum of marginal utilities: 12 plus 9 plus 7 plus 4 equals 32 utils. Summing rather than averaging is correct.
questions.hint: Add the marginal values.

questions.stem: In a ticket about a developer drinking water after exercise, explain why the marginal utility of each extra glass falls.

answer.exemplar: Each extra glass satisfies a less urgent need than the previous one, so added satisfaction falls while total utility still rises but at a decreasing rate.

questions.explanation: As consumption rises, each unit serves a less pressing want, so added satisfaction declines. Total utility can still rise, but more slowly.
questions.hint: Think about which need each unit satisfies.

questions.topic: Consumer surplus from a demand schedule
questions.learningObjective: Compute consumer surplus from a schedule

stimulus.body: A demand schedule lists willingness to pay of 12, 9 and 6 dollars for three units and the market price is 6 dollars. Derived from a sprint ticket scenario.

questions.stem: Given willingness to pay of 12, 9 and 6 dollars and a price of 6 dollars, what is consumer surplus?

options.text: 27 dollars, the sum of all willingness to pay values.
options.misconception: uses total willingness to pay as surplus

options.text: 15 dollars, from (12+9+6)-6.
0 dollars, because price equals the last willingness to pay.

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the sum of willingness to pay minus price for each unit bought: (12-6)+(9-6)+(6-6)=9 dollars. Summing willingness to pay or subtracting price once overstates or understates it.
questions.hint: Subtract price from each willingness to pay.

questions.topic: Marginal benefit and the demand curve
questions.stem: A product manager's ticket asks why the demand curve slopes downward; which reason is correct?

options.text: Because marginal benefit rises as more units are consumed.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of marginal benefit

options.text: Because consumers must buy all units at one price.
Because supply always equals demand at every price.
Because marginal benefit falls, so less is bought at high prices.

questions.explanation: The demand curve reflects falling marginal benefit: consumers value extra units less, so quantity demanded falls as price rises. Rising marginal benefit would slope demand upward.
questions.hint: Connect marginal benefit to willingness to pay.

questions.stem: A designer's ticket lists marginal utilities 8, 5, 2, -1 for four snacks; at which unit does satiation occur?
questions.explanation: Satiation occurs where marginal utility reaches zero or turns negative, here at the fourth unit with -1. The first three units still add positive satisfaction.
questions.hint: Find where marginal utility hits zero or below.

questions.stem: In a sprint ticket about a team's tool budget, the budget line represents which set of bundles?

options.text: All bundles that cost less than the team's income.
All bundles that cost exactly the team's income.
Bundles that maximize utility regardless of cost.
Bundles whose cost exceeds income but are still desired.

questions.explanation: The budget line is the set of bundles whose total cost equals income. Interior bundles are affordable but not on the line, and unaffordable bundles lie beyond it.
questions.hint: Think equality of cost and income.

questions.stem: Income is 60 dollars, good X costs 6 dollars and good Y costs 4 dollars; what is the X-intercept of the budget line?
questions.explanation: The X-intercept is income divided by the price of X: 60 divided by 6 equals 10 units. The Y-intercept would be 60 divided by 4.
questions.hint: Divide income by the X price.

questions.topic: Budget line response to a price change
questions.learningObjective: Predict budget line shift from price change
questions.stem: A ticket notes the price of good X falls while income and the price of Y stay fixed; what happens to the budget line?

options.text: It shifts inward parallel, reducing both intercepts.
options.misconception: confuses price fall with income fall

options.text: Both intercepts rise, shifting the line outward parallel.
options.misconception: treats a price change as an income change

options.text: The Y-intercept rises and the line pivots outward on the Y axis.
The X-intercept rises and the line pivots outward on the X axis.

questions.explanation: A fall in the price of X raises the X-intercept and pivots the budget line outward along the X axis while the Y-intercept stays fixed. Parallel shifts require income changes.
questions.hint: Only the intercept of the changed good moves.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish real income from relative prices
questions.stem: A reviewer's ticket says a price change alters both real income and relative prices; which effect changes real income?

options.text: The substitution effect, because relative prices changed.
The price effect, because the budget line pivoted.
options.misconception: names a combined rather than decomposed effect

options.text: The income effect, because purchasing power changed.
The wealth effect, because assets were repriced.

questions.explanation: The income effect captures the change in real purchasing power, while the substitution effect captures the response to changed relative prices. The combined price effect includes both.
questions.hint: Purchasing power is the income effect.

questions.learningObjective: Read optimal bundles at two prices

stimulus.body: A ticket shows a consumer choosing 6 of good X and 4 of good Y at old prices and 8 of X and 2 of Y at new prices. Quantities are in units per week.

questions.stem: At old prices the bundle is (6,4) and at new prices (8,2); which good became relatively cheaper?

options.text: Good Y, because its quantity fell.
options.misconception: reads quantity change as price change

options.text: Both, because both quantities changed.
Neither, because total spending is unchanged.
options.misconception: assumes constant spending means no price change

options.text: Good X, because its quantity rose.

questions.explanation: The consumer substitutes toward the good whose relative price fell, so rising quantity of X signals X became relatively cheaper. Quantity alone does not prove a price change without the budget constraint.
questions.hint: Substitution points to the cheaper good.

questions.topic: Substitution toward the relatively cheaper good
questions.stem: A developer's ticket raises the price of coffee relative to tea; according to the substitution effect, what happens?

options.text: The developer buys less coffee and more tea.
The developer buys more coffee and less tea.
The developer buys the same amounts of both.
The developer stops buying both drinks entirely.
options.misconception: overstates the effect of a relative change

questions.explanation: The substitution effect moves consumption away from the good that became relatively dearer and toward the relatively cheaper one. Buying more coffee would reverse the effect.
questions.hint: Substitute toward the cheaper good.

questions.topic: Total effect of a price change
questions.stem: A QA ticket shows the price of a normal good rises; the total effect on quantity demanded is which direction?

options.text: Quantity demanded rises because the income effect dominates.
options.misconception: predicts wrong direction for a normal good

options.text: Quantity demanded is unchanged because effects cancel.
Quantity demanded falls because both effects reduce it.
Quantity demanded rises because the substitution effect reverses.

questions.explanation: For a normal good, a price rise reduces quantity demanded through both the substitution effect and the income effect, so the total effect is a fall. Neither effect offsets or reverses.
questions.hint: Both effects point the same way for normal goods.

questions.stem: A ticket describes a staple food whose quantity demanded rises when its price rises; this is called what?

options.text: A normal good, because demand follows income.
An inferior good, because demand falls with income.
A luxury good, because spending share rises.
A Giffen good, because the income effect outweighs substitution.

questions.explanation: A Giffen good is an inferior good for which the income effect of a price rise outweighs the substitution effect, so quantity demanded rises with price. Inferiority alone is not sufficient.
questions.hint: The income effect must dominate.

questions.stem: In a ticket about a price drop for a normal good, explain how the total effect splits into income and substitution effects.

answer.exemplar: The substitution effect alone raises quantity demanded because the good is now relatively cheaper, and the income effect adds further demand because purchasing power rises; together they form the total effect.

questions.explanation: The substitution effect responds to the new relative price, and the income effect responds to higher real purchasing power. For a normal good both raise quantity demanded.
questions.hint: One effect is relative price, the other purchasing power.

questions.stem: A ticket shows a consumer chose bundle A when bundle B was affordable; what does revealed preference imply?

options.text: Bundle A is revealed preferred to bundle B.
Bundle B is revealed preferred to bundle A.
The consumer is indifferent between A and B.
Prices must have been equal for both bundles.

questions.explanation: When a consumer chooses A while B is affordable, A is revealed preferred to B. Indifference or reversed preference would contradict the observed choice.
questions.hint: Choice reveals preference.

questions.stem: A ticket reprices a bundle originally costing 40 dollars at new prices costing 50 dollars; income is 55 dollars; is the bundle still affordable?
questions.explanation: The repriced bundle costs 50 dollars against income of 55 dollars, so it is affordable; code 1 means affordable and 0 means not. Affordability requires cost not to exceed income.
questions.hint: Compare repriced cost to income.

questions.topic: The weak axiom of revealed preference
questions.stem: A ticket asks for the weak axiom of revealed preference; which statement is correct?

options.text: Revealed preference requires equal prices for all goods.
If A is revealed preferred to B, then B must be revealed preferred to A.
A and B are always revealed indifferent when affordable.
If A is revealed preferred to B, then B cannot be revealed preferred to A.

questions.explanation: The weak axiom says revealed preference is asymmetric: if A is revealed preferred to B, B cannot be revealed preferred to A. Reversal or indifference claims violate it.
questions.hint: Preference cannot run both ways.

questions.topic: Spotting a weak axiom violation in data

stimulus.body: A ticket lists two observed choices: bundle (4,2) chosen when (2,4) was affordable, and (2,4) chosen when (4,2) was affordable. Quantities are units of two goods.

questions.stem: Does this data violate the weak axiom of revealed preference?

options.text: No, because prices might have changed.
options.misconception: ignores that affordability is already given

options.text: No, because quantities differ between observations.
Yes, because each bundle is revealed preferred to the other.
Yes, because total spending differs across bundles.
options.misconception: uses spending equality as the test

questions.explanation: Each bundle is revealed preferred to the other, which violates the weak axiom. Price changes do not excuse the violation once affordability is established.
questions.hint: Check for mutual revealed preference.

questions.learningObjective: State what revealed preference can establish
questions.stem: A ticket asks what revealed preference alone can determine; which claim is valid?

options.text: It can determine exact utility numbers for each bundle.
It can recover the consumer's income level.
options.misconception: income is not revealed by choices alone

options.text: It can prove the consumer maximizes profit.
It can establish ordinal rankings among observed bundles.

questions.explanation: Revealed preference yields ordinal rankings among observed bundles, not cardinal utility, income, or profit maximization. Exact utility numbers require stronger assumptions.
questions.hint: Ordinal, not cardinal.

questions.stem: A ticket records a consumer buying 5 units at 4 dollars and 3 units at 6 dollars; if income is fully spent, what is income?
questions.explanation: Income equals total expenditure: 5 times 4 plus 3 times 6 equals 20 plus 18, which is 38 dollars. Full spending is assumed.
questions.hint: Multiply quantities by prices and sum.

questions.stem: A ticket about a developer selling a plugin asks what producer surplus measures; which answer is correct?

options.text: The total revenue from all units sold.
The difference between price received and average cost.
options.misconception: confuses surplus with profit per unit

options.text: The difference between price received and minimum acceptable price.
The cost of producing all units sold.

questions.explanation: Producer surplus is price received minus the minimum acceptable price for each unit. It differs from profit, which subtracts average or total cost, and from revenue or cost alone.
questions.hint: Minimum acceptable price is the supply curve.

questions.learningObjective: Compute producer surplus as a triangle
questions.stem: Price is 10 dollars, minimum acceptable price at zero quantity is 4 dollars, and quantity sold is 12 units; what is producer surplus as a triangle?
questions.explanation: Producer surplus is half the base times height: 0.5 times 12 times (10-4) equals 36 dollars. The height is price minus the supply intercept.
questions.hint: Use one-half base times height.

questions.stem: A ticket compares producer surplus and profit for a firm; which statement is correct?

options.text: They are identical measures with different names.
Producer surplus is always smaller than profit.
Profit includes fixed costs but producer surplus does not.
Producer surplus equals profit when fixed costs are zero.

questions.explanation: Producer surplus excludes fixed costs, while profit subtracts all costs including fixed costs; they coincide only when fixed costs are zero. Surplus is generally larger than profit.
questions.hint: Fixed costs separate the two measures.

questions.stem: A ticket asks when a firm should shut down in the short run; which condition is correct?

options.text: Shut down when price is below average total cost.
Shut down when price is below marginal cost.
Shut down when price is below average variable cost.
Shut down when total revenue is below total cost.

questions.explanation: A firm shuts down in the short run when price falls below average variable cost, because it cannot cover variable costs. Price below average total cost means a loss but not necessarily shutdown.
questions.hint: Variable costs are the relevant threshold.

questions.topic: Price against average variable and total cost
questions.stem: A ticket gives price 8 dollars, average variable cost 6 dollars and average total cost 10 dollars; what is the firm's best short-run action?

options.text: Produce at maximum capacity regardless of cost.
Shut down immediately, because price is below average total cost.
Raise price to cover average total cost.
Continue producing, because price exceeds average variable cost.

questions.explanation: Since price exceeds average variable cost but is below average total cost, the firm minimizes loss by continuing to produce in the short run. Shutting down would lose all fixed costs.
questions.hint: Compare price to average variable cost first.

questions.topic: Producer surplus and gains from trade
questions.learningObjective: Link producer surplus to gains from trade
questions.stem: A ticket asks why producer surplus represents gains from trade; which explanation is correct?

options.text: It measures the tax collected on sales.
It measures revenue minus total cost.
It measures units sold above the minimum acceptable price.
It measures consumer willingness to pay.

questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the gain from trade because it is the excess of price over the minimum acceptable price for units sold. Revenue minus total cost is profit, not surplus.
questions.hint: Surplus is price minus minimum acceptable price.

questions.learningObjective: Apply diminishing marginal utility to a new good
questions.stem: In a ticket about a QA engineer eating slices of pizza, the fourth slice adds less satisfaction than the first; this illustrates what?

options.text: Increasing marginal utility of food.
Zero marginal utility at every slice.
Constant total utility across slices.
Diminishing marginal utility of food.

questions.explanation: When later units add less satisfaction than earlier ones, marginal utility is diminishing. Total utility still rises, just more slowly.
questions.hint: Compare added satisfaction across units.

questions.stem: A ticket records total utilities of 10 and 17 utils for 2 and 3 units; what is marginal utility of the third unit?
questions.explanation: Marginal utility of the third unit is total utility at 3 minus total at 2: 17 minus 10 equals 7 utils. Subtracting in the correct order matters.
questions.hint: Subtract the previous total.

stimulus.body: A ticket shows good A with marginal utility 12 and price 3, and good B with marginal utility 15 and price 5. Quantities are per unit of each good.

questions.stem: Which good has higher marginal utility per dollar?

options.text: Good A, at 12 utils per dollar.
Good B, at 3 utils per dollar.
Good A, at 4 utils per dollar.
Good B, at 15 utils per dollar.

questions.explanation: Good A yields 12 divided by 3, or 4 utils per dollar, and good B yields 15 divided by 5, or 3 utils per dollar, so A is higher. Using marginal utility alone would misrank.
questions.hint: Divide marginal utility by price for each good.

questions.stem: A ticket shows a consumer with marginal utility 10 and price 10 for good X and marginal utility 8 and price 6 for good Y; should they buy more X?

options.text: Yes, because marginal utility of X exceeds its price.
No, because price of X is too high.
Yes, because marginal utility of Y is lower.
No, because marginal utility equals price for X.

questions.explanation: When marginal utility equals price for X, the consumer is at the optimum for that good and should not buy more X. Comparing Y or misreading the equality would lead to errors.
questions.hint: Check whether marginal utility equals price.

questions.stem: A ticket asks what happens to total utility when marginal utility is zero; which answer is correct?

options.text: Total utility is falling.
options.misconception: confuses zero marginal with negative marginal

options.text: Total utility is zero.
options.misconception: confuses marginal zero with total zero

options.text: Total utility is maximized.
Total utility is undefined.

questions.explanation: When marginal utility is zero, total utility is at its maximum because additional units add nothing. Total utility is not zero unless no units were consumed.
questions.hint: Zero marginal means no further gain.

questions.learningObjective: Apply diminishing marginal utility to services
questions.stem: A ticket about a developer's coffee consumption asks why the fifth cup adds less satisfaction than the first.

answer.exemplar: The first cup relieves strong fatigue while later cups satisfy weaker wants, so added satisfaction declines even though total satisfaction still rises.

questions.explanation: Early units satisfy urgent needs and later units satisfy weaker ones, so marginal utility falls. Total utility can still increase, just more slowly.
questions.hint: Match units to need urgency.

questions.topic: Consumer surplus from a demand schedule
questions.learningObjective: Compute consumer surplus at a new price
questions.stem: A ticket lists willingness to pay 15, 11 and 7 dollars and price 7 dollars; what is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is (15-7)+(11-7)+(7-7), which equals 8 plus 4 plus 0, or 12 dollars. Each unit's surplus is willingness to pay minus price.
questions.hint: Subtract price from each willingness to pay.

questions.topic: Marginal benefit and the demand curve
questions.stem: A ticket asks what price a consumer will pay for an extra unit; which concept applies?

options.text: The marginal cost of producing the unit.
options.misconception: uses producer rather than consumer concept

options.text: The total cost of production.
The average cost of all units.
The marginal benefit of consuming the unit.

questions.explanation: A consumer's willingness to pay for an extra unit equals its marginal benefit. Marginal cost, average cost, and total cost are producer-side concepts.
questions.hint: Willingness to pay reflects marginal benefit.

questions.stem: A ticket records marginal utilities 6, 3, 0, -2; at which unit is total utility maximized?

options.text: At the first unit, because marginal utility is highest.
options.misconception: confuses highest marginal with maximum total

options.text: At the fourth unit, because total utility is largest.
At the third unit, because marginal utility is zero.
At the second unit, because marginal utility equals price.

questions.explanation: Total utility is maximized where marginal utility reaches zero, here at the third unit. The fourth unit reduces total utility because its marginal utility is negative.
questions.hint: Zero marginal utility marks the peak.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the slope of the budget line
questions.stem: Good X costs 5 dollars and good Y costs 10 dollars; what is the slope of the budget line in absolute value?
questions.explanation: The slope's absolute value is the price of X divided by the price of Y: 5 divided by 10 equals 0.5. This reflects the relative price of X in terms of Y.
questions.hint: Divide the X price by the Y price.

questions.stem: Income is 80 dollars and good Y costs 8 dollars; what is the Y-intercept of the budget line?
questions.explanation: The Y-intercept is income divided by the price of Y: 80 divided by 8 equals 10 units. The X-intercept would use the price of X instead.
questions.hint: Divide income by the Y price.

questions.topic: Budget line response to a price change
questions.learningObjective: Predict parallel shift from income change
questions.stem: A ticket notes income rises while both prices stay fixed; what happens to the budget line?

options.text: It pivots outward on the X axis only.
options.misconception: confuses income change with price change

options.text: It becomes steeper without shifting.
options.misconception: confuses income change with relative price change

options.text: It shifts inward parallel, lowering both intercepts.
It shifts outward parallel, raising both intercepts.

questions.explanation: An income increase shifts the budget line outward in parallel, raising both intercepts while the slope stays the same. Pivots require price changes.
questions.hint: Income changes shift, prices pivot.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which effect changes relative prices
questions.stem: A ticket decomposes a price change; which effect captures the change in relative prices?

options.text: The income effect, because purchasing power changes.
The total effect, because it combines both.
options.misconception: names the aggregate, not the component

options.text: The substitution effect, because relative prices changed.
The wealth effect, because assets were repriced.

questions.explanation: The substitution effect captures the response to changed relative prices, while the income effect captures changed purchasing power. The total effect combines both.
questions.hint: Relative prices belong to substitution.

questions.learningObjective: Infer price change from choice data

stimulus.body: A ticket shows a consumer choosing (4,6) at old prices and (6,4) at new prices, with income unchanged. Quantities are units per period.

questions.stem: Which good became relatively cheaper between the two observations?

options.text: Good Y, because its quantity fell.
options.misconception: reads quantity change as price change for the wrong good

options.text: Both, because both quantities changed.
Neither, because income is unchanged.
options.misconception: confuses income constancy with no price change

options.text: Good X, because its quantity rose.

questions.explanation: Substitution toward X indicates X became relatively cheaper. Income constancy does not imply unchanged prices; the budget line can pivot.
questions.hint: Rising quantity signals the cheaper good.

questions.topic: Substitution toward the relatively cheaper good
questions.learningObjective: Apply substitution to a price rise
questions.stem: A ticket raises the price of tea relative to coffee; the substitution effect predicts which change?

options.text: Less tea and more coffee.
More tea and less coffee.
Equal amounts of both drinks.
No purchases of either drink.

questions.explanation: The substitution effect moves consumption away from the relatively dearer good and toward the cheaper one, so less tea and more coffee. Equal or zero purchases would ignore the price change.
questions.hint: Substitute toward the cheaper good.

questions.topic: Total effect of a price change
questions.learningObjective: Predict total effect for an inferior good
questions.stem: A ticket raises the price of an inferior good; the income effect works in which direction on quantity demanded?

options.text: It leaves quantity demanded unchanged.
It decreases quantity demanded, reinforcing substitution.
It increases quantity demanded, opposing substitution.
It reverses the substitution effect entirely.

questions.explanation: For an inferior good, a price rise reduces real income and, because demand falls as income rises, quantity demanded rises, opposing the substitution effect. Reinforcement would describe a normal good.
questions.hint: Inferior goods have opposite income response.

questions.learningObjective: Identify conditions for a Giffen good
questions.stem: A ticket asks which condition must hold for a Giffen good; which is necessary?

options.text: The good must have zero income elasticity.
The good must be normal and the substitution effect must dominate.
The good must be a luxury with high income elasticity.
The good must be inferior and the income effect must dominate.

questions.explanation: A Giffen good must be inferior and the income effect must dominate the substitution effect. Normal goods, luxuries, and zero-elasticity goods do not qualify.
questions.hint: Inferiority plus dominance.

questions.stem: A ticket asks how total effect relates to income and substitution effects; which equation is correct?

options.text: Total effect equals substitution effect only.
Total effect equals income effect minus substitution effect.
Total effect equals income effect plus substitution effect.
Total effect equals income effect only.

questions.explanation: The total effect of a price change equals the sum of the income effect and the substitution effect. Omitting either or subtracting would misstate the decomposition.
questions.hint: Add the two components.

questions.learningObjective: Apply revealed preference to a new choice
questions.stem: A ticket shows a consumer chose bundle X when bundle Y was affordable; what is revealed?

options.text: Bundle Y is preferred to bundle X.
Prices of X and Y were equal.
The consumer is indifferent between X and Y.
Bundle X is preferred to bundle Y.

questions.explanation: Choosing X when Y is affordable reveals X is preferred to Y. Indifference or price equality would not follow from the observation alone.
questions.hint: Choice reveals strict preference.

questions.stem: A bundle of 3 units at 4 dollars and 2 units at 5 dollars is repriced to 5 and 6 dollars respectively; what is the new cost?
questions.explanation: Repriced cost is 3 times 5 plus 2 times 6, which equals 15 plus 12, or 27 dollars. Multiply each quantity by its new price.
questions.hint: Multiply quantities by new prices.

questions.topic: The weak axiom of revealed preference
questions.learningObjective: Test the weak axiom with data

stimulus.body: A ticket lists choice 1: bundle (3,3) when (1,5) affordable; choice 2: bundle (1,5) when (3,3) affordable. Quantities are units of two goods.

questions.stem: Does this pair of choices violate the weak axiom?

options.text: No, because prices could have changed.
No, because the quantities sum to six in both cases.
Yes, because each bundle is revealed preferred to the other.
Yes, because total spending differs.

questions.explanation: Each bundle is revealed preferred to the other, violating the weak axiom. Spending differences or price changes do not override established affordability.
questions.hint: Look for mutual revealed preference.

questions.topic: Spotting a weak axiom violation in data

stimulus.body: A ticket lists choice 1: bundle (5,1) when (2,4) affordable; choice 2: bundle (2,4) when (5,1) is not affordable. Quantities are units of two goods.

questions.stem: Does this data violate the weak axiom?

options.text: Yes, because spending differs across bundles.
No, because prices must have been equal.
Yes, because quantities changed between observations.
No, because the second bundle was not affordable in choice 1's situation.

questions.explanation: No violation occurs because the second observation does not reveal preference over the first bundle, since that bundle was unaffordable. Quantity change or spending alone does not establish violation.
questions.hint: Check affordability in each observation.

questions.learningObjective: State the limits of revealed preference
questions.stem: A ticket asks what revealed preference cannot determine; which limitation is correct?

options.text: It cannot apply to more than two goods.
It cannot compare bundles with different goods.
It cannot rank bundles that were never both affordable.
It cannot use observed choices at all.

questions.explanation: Revealed preference only ranks bundles that were directly comparable through affordability; unrelated bundles cannot be ranked. It applies to many goods and uses observed choices.
questions.hint: Ranking requires direct comparability.

questions.stem: A ticket records a consumer buying 4 units at 7 dollars and 2 units at 9 dollars with full spending; what is income?
questions.explanation: Income equals 4 times 7 plus 2 times 9, which is 28 plus 18, or 46 dollars. Full spending means expenditure equals income.
questions.hint: Multiply and sum expenditures.

questions.learningObjective: Compute producer surplus from a schedule

stimulus.body: A ticket lists minimum acceptable prices of 4, 6 and 8 dollars for three units and a market price of 9 dollars. Quantities are units per period.

questions.stem: What is producer surplus at a price of 9 dollars?

options.text: 21 dollars, from 9 times 3 minus 6.
27 dollars, the sum of all minimum prices.
options.misconception: sums minimum prices instead of surpluses

options.text: 9 dollars, using price alone.

questions.explanation: Producer surplus is (9-4)+(9-6)+(9-8), which equals 5 plus 3 plus 1, or 9 dollars. Each unit's surplus is market price minus minimum acceptable price.
questions.hint: Subtract minimum price from market price for each unit.

questions.learningObjective: Compute producer surplus triangle with new values
questions.stem: Price is 14 dollars, supply intercept is 6 dollars, and quantity is 8 units; what is producer surplus?
questions.explanation: Producer surplus equals 0.5 times 8 times (14-6), which is 0.5 times 8 times 8, or 32 dollars. Half base times height is the triangle area.
questions.hint: Use one-half base times height.

questions.stem: A ticket shows producer surplus of 50 dollars and fixed costs of 12 dollars; what is profit?
questions.explanation: Profit equals producer surplus minus fixed costs: 50 minus 12 equals 38 dollars. Fixed costs separate producer surplus from profit.
questions.hint: Subtract fixed costs from surplus.

questions.learningObjective: Apply shutdown condition to a case
questions.stem: A ticket gives price 5 dollars and average variable cost 7 dollars; should the firm produce in the short run?

options.text: Yes, because price is positive.
Yes, because price exceeds marginal cost.
No, because price is below average variable cost.
No, because price is below average total cost.

questions.explanation: When price is below average variable cost, the firm should shut down in the short run. Price below average total cost alone means a loss but not shutdown.
questions.hint: Compare price to average variable cost.

questions.topic: Price against average variable and total cost

stimulus.body: A ticket shows price 9 dollars, average variable cost 7 dollars and average total cost 11 dollars. All values are in dollars per unit.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the firm's short-run situation?

options.text: The firm makes a profit.
options.misconception: ignores that price is below ATC

options.text: The firm breaks even.
The firm should shut down immediately.
The firm minimizes loss by producing.

questions.explanation: Price exceeds average variable cost but is below average total cost, so the firm minimizes loss by producing. Profit, break-even, and shutdown do not fit.
questions.hint: Compare price to AVC and ATC.

questions.topic: Producer surplus and gains from trade
questions.learningObjective: Explain producer surplus as gain from trade
questions.stem: A ticket asks why producer surplus is called a gain from trade; explain in one or two sentences.

answer.exemplar: Producers receive more than their minimum acceptable price for units sold, so the difference is a gain created by trading at the market price.

questions.explanation: Producer surplus measures the excess of market price over the minimum acceptable price, which is the gain from trade. Without trade, producers would only get their minimum.
questions.hint: Compare market price to minimum acceptable price.
